name: Facial analysis YouTube channels

lead: Facial analysis channels are creators who assess faces on video or livestream, rating features such as eye tilt, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like PSL. Viewers use them to learn where their face stands and what to change.

The chain: creators rate eyes, jaw and cheeks, viewers learn which features hold their look back, then choose changes from skincare to surgery. The ratings are not scientifically validated, and critics call parts of the scale pseudoscientific. No studies have examined the content or its viewers.

paras: Viewers submit photos for review, follow breakdowns of their features and watch before-and-after comparisons. Creators assign a tier or score and suggest changes, which viewers pair with grooming, fitness, skincare or procedures.
Press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. Critics describe PSL-style ratings as pseudoscientific.

angle.text: Viewers watch creators rate faces on feature scales such as PSL to learn which features to improve and how. The ratings are not scientifically validated, and press coverage links the content to body-image concerns.

lead: Facial analysis content is video and livestream material in which creators assess faces, rating features such as eye shape, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like the PSL scale. Viewers submit photos or watch breakdowns to learn which features a creator thinks are strengths or weak points and what could be changed, from haircut, skincare and weight to surgery. It is a staple of looksmaxxing culture online.[1]

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes the practice as spreading from incel-era forums to TikTok in the 2020s and names livestreamers such as Clavicular and Androgenic; it does not discuss YouTube channels specifically.[1] Critics describe PSL-style ratings as pseudoscientific, while some men report benefits such as improved confidence.[1]

Academic research on facial attractiveness examines features such as symmetry, averageness, youthfulness, sexual dimorphism and skin quality, which overlap with what the channels discuss.[2][3] No studies have examined facial analysis channels or their viewers.

paras: Content in this category assesses features believed to affect attractiveness, such as positive canthal tilt ('hunter eyes'), hollow cheeks and a defined jawline, and often places faces on a tier scale. Sources disagree on the tiers; one overview lists seven, from 'subhuman' to 'giga Chad', while another lists three.[1]

Researchers studying facial attractiveness have examined symmetry, averageness, youthfulness (neoteny), sexual dimorphism and skin quality, along with eye spacing and shape, lip fullness, jaw and chin shape and cheekbones.[3] Wikipedia's facial symmetry article reports that more symmetrical faces are rated as more attractive and healthier, and that symmetry and averageness contribute independently.[2] Some researchers report broad cross-cultural agreement on what makes a face attractive, while the same article notes that findings are more limited in places and ideals have changed over time.[3] Channels use community vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes rather than these research terms.

The term looksmaxxing was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s, and early culture was shaped by forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, now defunct.[1] The trend was popularized on TikTok in the 2020s and covered by outlets including the New York Times and Business Insider in November 2023.[1]

Commentators and researchers describe the practice as judgmental and reliant on anecdote.[1] Reports in outlets including the BBC and Guardian have linked communities that rate appearance with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and one researcher argues algorithms can draw young men toward incel views.[1]

No studies found on facial analysis channels. Related academic research on rating faces uses photographs, composites, 3D models and brief exposures, as described in the encyclopedia overview of facial attractiveness.[3]

timeline.event: The term looksmaxxing is coined on incel message boards.[1]
Mainstream press covers the TikTok looksmaxxing trend.[1]
Livestreamers such as Clavicular and Androgenic receive wide press coverage.[1]
